analysis.title: Weekly Economic Perspectives (October 30, 2026)
key_insights: Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% with two dissents favoring a hike (Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack). The author calls a December hike more or less a given, with risks being a major risk-off move or Iran re-escalation.
US Q3 GDP grew 3.4% saar versus a 3.2% consensus estimate and 2.2% prior. Consumption grew 3.8% saar and added 2.5 ppts to growth.

Private investment rose 19.4% saar, with half of that from inventories. Private fixed investment grew 9.4%, led by computers and peripheral equipment at +66.7% saar. Residential construction contracted again.
Net trade subtracted 3.3 ppts from Q3 growth, the worst on record apart from the Q1 2025 tariff-driven spike. Surging imports were tied directly to AI investment.
Real GDP grew 2.3% y/y over the first three quarters, matching the author's full-year target held since last December.
The Bank of Canada hiked 25 bp to 2.50% in a move the author says surprised them but not markets. The author expects one more 25 bp hike to 2.75% in December or January, then a pause.
The BoC expects Brent to average about US$100 a barrel in Q4, falling to about US$75 by end-2028. The author forecasts 2027 Canadian growth of 1.3% versus the BoC's 2%.

The ECB held at 2.65%. The author sees another hike in December as more likely than not and expects the cycle to be capped at one additional hike. Lagarde confirmed she will leave early next February.

The BoJ held at 1.25% with one dissent for a 25 bp hike. The author still expects two more hikes over the next nine months but sees weak Q3 GDP as an argument for patience on timing. The November 16 GDP release is the key input.

Australian Sep CPI rose 4.3% y/y with quarterly trimmed mean at 1.0% q/q, services at 4.1% and non-tradables at 4.5%. The author expects a 25 bp RBA hike next week to 4.85%, with a 20% chance of a hold, and a cash rate that can reach 5%.

tension_points.bull_case: Underlying inflation is consistent with the 2% target and the BoJ is confident it is sustainable, which supports further hikes. The author expects two more hikes over the next nine months.
tension_points.bear_case: Q3 GDP is expected to be weak, with softer consumption and net exports subtracting from growth. Real purchasing power is eroding, which argues for waiting.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If the November 16 Q3 GDP release confirms weakness in consumption and trade volumes, the case for waiting becomes materially stronger.

tension_points.bull_case: Inflation remains elevated, with services at 4.1% and non-tradables at 4.5%. The author expects another 25 bp hike next week and a cash rate that can reach 5%.
tension_points.bear_case: Unemployment is near 4.8%, sentiment is weak and cumulative tightening is weighing on leveraged households. A 20% chance of a hold is assigned for next week.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A hold next week, or more weakness in unemployment and demand, would signal growing caution around cumulative tightening.
